# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

### Introduction and Rationale
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major contributor to ischemic stroke, with thrombus formation occurring predominantly (up to 90%) within the left atrial appendage (LAA) in patients with non-valvular AF [1]. The LAA exhibits high morphological heterogeneity, commonly classified into chicken wing, cactus, windsock, and cauliflower shapes [2]. Complex, multi-lobed structures are associated with a higher thromboembolic risk due to stasis and slow-flow hemodynamics [2]. Consequently, excluding the LAA from the systemic circulation has become a key non-pharmacological strategy for stroke prevention, particularly for patients who cannot tolerate long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC).

### Pre-Procedural and Intra-Procedural Imaging
Precise pre-procedural planning and real-time intra-procedural guidance are critical to the safety and success of percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC). Pre-procedural cardiac computed tomography (CT) has emerged as an invaluable tool, enabling high-resolution characterization of the LAA ostium, landing zone, and accessory lobes, which facilitates precise device sizing and minimizes procedural failures [3]. During the implantation, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains the standard of care for guiding the transseptal puncture and evaluating device positioning, compression, and sealing. However, intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) is increasingly adopted as an alternative, offering comparable success rates and minimizing the need for general anesthesia or tracheal intubation [4].

### Pivotal Trial Evidence and Registries
The clinical efficacy of percutaneous LAAC was first established in the landmark PROTECT AF trial, which showed that occlusion with the first-generation Watchman device (Boston Scientific) was non-inferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death [5]. The subsequent PREVAIL trial evaluated the device in patients at higher risk of thromboembolism, demonstrating improved procedural safety as operator experience grew [6]. Patient-level meta-analyses [7] and long-term 5-year outcomes from these trials [8] confirmed that LAAC significantly reduced hemorrhagic stroke, non-procedural bleeding, and cardiovascular mortality compared to warfarin.

In real-world settings, the EWOLUTION registry demonstrated a high implant success rate (98.5%) and a low post-procedural complication rate in a broad, high-bleeding-risk European population [9]. The ASAP study showed that LAAC was safe and effective in patients with absolute contraindications to oral anticoagulants using a post-implant regimen of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) [10]. More recently, the large-scale National Cardiovascular Data Registry (NCDR) LAAO Registry confirmed a high contemporary procedural success rate (>98%) in clinical practice [11], although analysis of this registry highlighted important sex-based differences in procedural outcomes and complications [12].

### Device Evolution and Head-to-Head Comparisons
Technological iterations have sought to optimize device design and reduce complications. Integrating pre-procedural 3D CT planning significantly shortens the operator learning curve and improves sizing accuracy [13]. The next-generation Watchman FLX device, featuring a fully enclosed distal end, demonstrated excellent safety and high rates of effective LAA occlusion in the PINNACLE FLX trial [14]. Concurrently, the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott), which employs a disc-and-lobe dual-seal design, was validated in the Amulet IDE trial, demonstrating non-inferiority to the first-generation Watchman with superior immediate LAA closure rates [15]. Head-to-head evaluation in the SWISS-APERO trial showed higher rates of complete LAA occlusion with the Amulet device compared to Watchman [16], a benefit that persisted at 1 year [17]. For complex or highly lobulated LAA anatomies, other specialized devices, such as the LAmbre device, also offer highly effective occlusion [18].

### Comparison with Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs)
With DOACs establishing themselves as the pharmacological standard of care, several clinical trials have compared them directly to percutaneous LAAC. The PRAGUE-17 trial demonstrated that LAAC was non-inferior to DOACs in high-risk AF patients at both short-term [19] and 4-year long-term follow-up [20]. More recently, the OPTION trial showed that in patients undergoing catheter ablation for AF, LAAC with the Watchman FLX device was non-inferior to DOACs for the primary efficacy composite while significantly reducing non-procedural major and clinically relevant bleeding at 3 years [21]. The landmark CHAMPION-AF trial confirmed that LAA closure was non-inferior to DOAC therapy for efficacy (cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism) and superior in reducing non-procedural bleeding over a 3-year follow-up period [22]. The ongoing CATALYST trial will soon provide similar comparative data for the Amulet device against DOACs [23].

### Complications, Management, and Guidelines
Despite advancements, procedural and device-specific challenges remain. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in approximately 3-4% of patients and increases ischemic stroke risk [24]. Furthermore, residual peri-device leaks (PDLs), even if small (≤3 mm), are associated with a significant increase in thromboembolic events over 5 years [25]. Consequently, contemporary expert consensus statements from the European Heart Rhythm Association (EHRA) and European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) emphasize tailored post-procedural antithrombotic therapy and regular surveillance imaging [26].

Current European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [27] and American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guidelines [28] recommend percutaneous LAAC (Class IIb) for AF patients with contraindications to long-term anticoagulation. The validity of mechanical LAA exclusion is further reinforced by surgical evidence from the LAAOS III trial, which showed a 37% stroke reduction when the LAA was closed during concomitant cardiac surgery [29]. Finally, cost-effectiveness analyses show that percutaneous LAAC represents a highly cost-effective strategy, achieving economic dominance over both warfarin and DOACs within 5 to 10 years [30].
